Margaret Sanger. Born in 1879, the American birth control activist who devoted her life to making contraception legal, accessible, and normalized.

Working as a nurse on the Lower East Side of New York, Sanger witnessed firsthand the human cost of uncontrolled fertility. She treated women suffering from dangerous self-induced abortions and complications from repeated pregnancies. She realized that without access to contraception, women could not be truly free. This became the cornerstone of her activism.

In 1916, she opened the first birth control clinic in America in Brooklyn. She was arrested and imprisoned for distributing contraceptives, which violated the Comstock Laws. She coined the term "birth control," reframing contraception from moral transgression into a public health necessity and a woman's right.

Sanger founded what would become Planned Parenthood, an organization providing contraception, sex education, and reproductive healthcare to millions of women. She traveled internationally to promote family planning, particularly in the developing world, though her later advocacy became complicated by concerns about race and coercion. Her work was foundational to the sexual revolution and to women's liberation movements. Without access to contraception, feminists argued, women could not control their own destinies or participate fully in society.
